narrative: The model estimated a 52.0% probability that you will fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means failure was judged slightly more likely than passing; it is not a certainty, but it was high enough for the school to deny admission under its risk threshold. Your LSAT score was the most influential factor. At 42, above the 37.18 average among accepted students, it pushed toward passing. The second most influential factor was your third-year class rank decile. At 2, well below the accepted average of 5.79, it pushed toward failure. The third was your undergraduate GPA. At 2.40, below the accepted average of 3.23, it also pushed toward failure. Because two of the three strongest signals pointed toward failure, they outweighed the favorable LSAT signal and tipped the overall assessment above the school’s acceptable risk level. Your gender and race were not used. You should ask admissions whether an appeal or reconsideration process exists and submit a concise explanation of the low third-year rank and GPA, including any upward trend or extenuating circumstances. If reapplying, strengthen your academic record with rigorous upper-level or graduate coursework, seek bar-readiness advising, and consider a program with structured bar support.
